title: The earth disc: one thing for a jumping eye
hookLine: eyes jump on a train; Buddhaghosa gives them one disc of dawn-colored clay, and Patanjali's Yoga Sutras know the move
carry: kasina: one plain thing steadies the mind
tomorrow: after earth, the next disc is water. what changes?

cards: Watch someone's eyes on a train: window, phone, ad, a stranger's shoes, phone again. Eyes jump. Buddhaghosa's first subject on the list asks them to stop.
Make a disc of clay, he says, the color of the dawn sky, with every pebble and root picked out, smooth as a drum. Set it in front of you, and look. Just that.
So how could staring at clay calm anyone down? His answer, in one line: give the jumping eye one plain thing, and the mind follows the eye.

teach.b: The word is kasina: a disc or field used as the object of meditation. Earth is the first of ten.
You sit a little way off, eyes open gently, the way you'd look at your face in a mirror, and repeat a name for it softly: earth, earth. Not the color, not the clay. Just the plain fact of earth.

teach.h: THE IMAGE STAYS: THE LEARNING SIGN.
teach.b: After a while the image stays even when you close your eyes. Buddhaghosa calls that the learning sign.

Keep going, and a clearer image can arise, smooth as a mirror taken out of its case, or the moon coming out from behind a cloud. Steadiness like that is the calm. A neighbor tradition knows this move well.

teach.h: PATANJALI: BIND THE MIND TO ONE PLACE.
teach.b: In the Yoga Sutras, the Hindu teacher Patanjali calls it dharana: binding the mind to one place. Different tradition, the same discovery: a mind given one thing to rest on starts to settle. And the honest difference.

teach.h: TWO HOPES ABOUT WHERE IT LEADS.
teach.b: For Patanjali, that steadiness leads toward the seer resting in its own true nature.
For Buddhaghosa, the calm of the earth disc becomes a base for insight: seeing that nothing, not even the one looking, is a fixed self, the same search that closed Shantideva's guide.
One steady gaze, two different hopes about where it leads.

how: Kasina practice is taught in some Theravada meditation traditions, using a prepared disc or a natural field such as a plowed field; Hindu yoga traditions teach dharana, fixing attention on one place, as a limb of Patanjali's path.

o: a round cushion monks sit on during long sittings
a clay offering bowl placed in front of a shrine
a disc or field you gaze at to steady the mind

games.q: your yoga teacher says, "rest your gaze on one point." your friend asks: "so is that the Buddhist earth disc?" what's the fairest answer?
o: both steady the mind on one thing, with different hopes about where it leads.
yes, exactly the same; all meditation is one practice underneath.

games.why: the shared discovery is real: one object settles the mind. the difference is real too: Patanjali's seer at rest, Buddhaghosa's insight into no fixed self.

practice: Find something round and plain within sight: a plate, a coaster, the bottom of a mug. Look at it softly, the way you'd look at your face in a mirror, and name it inwardly, earth, or simply round.
When you're ready, close your eyes and see whether the shape stays; when it fades, open them and look again.

wordCard.voice: Kasina: a disc or field used as a meditation object. Earth comes first, a disc of dawn-colored clay.

orig.note: Pali: a whole field or disc used as a meditation object. Earth (पथवी, pathavi) is the first.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: the kasina, one plain thing to steady a jumping eye and mind. Six of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IV.21–31 (the earth kasina: dawn-colored clay, looking as at a face in a mirror, naming 'earth, earth', the learning sign and the counterpart sign)
Yoga Sutras 3.1 (dharana is binding the mind to one place) and 1.3 (then the seer rests in its own nature)
